newsitem.title: SPAIN: U.S. yacht rescues reed boat crew in Pacific.
newsitem.headline: U.S. yacht rescues reed boat crew in Pacific.

text.p: The stranded crew of a Spanish-led expedition which had hoped to sail round the world in a primitive reed raft was rescued on Sunday, two days after the vessel was split by a storm in a remote corner of the Pacific.

Relatives and friends of Spanish skipper Kitin Munoz in Madrid said he and his 12-member crew were all safe after a private U.S. yacht, the Stray Dog, answered a distress call to Chilean maritime authorities on Easter Island.
"They were rescued this morning at six Madrid time (0400 GMT). They are in good shape and in good spirits," Jose Munoz, brother of the skipper, told Reuters.
The crew of 10 Polynesians, two Bolivian Indians and the Spaniard, is expected to return on Sunday night to Chile's Easter Island from where the expedition was launched on May 5.
Jose Munoz said the crew had survived by staying afloat for two days and two nights on a makeshift raft of reeds cobbled together from remains of the broken ship.
"They had to work every hour to keep the raft from falling apart so it was important they were found quickly," he said.
The 99-foot (30-metre)-long Mata Rangi (Eyes of Paradise) set sail from Easter Island nearly three weeks ago using only primitive methods to sail around the world.
The ship, built by Bolivian Indians and Easter Islanders, was modeled after ancient Incan boats in an attempt to show primitive cultures could cross oceans, Jose Munoz said.
But it was modern technology that saved the crew's lives.
The skipper used a navigation instrument to send out a distress signal which Easter Island maritime authorities picked up, his brother said. The signal gave precise coordinates of their location.
"Without that, it would have been very difficult to locate a small boat in the middle of the ocean," Jose Munoz said.
Munoz said his brother had also used a satellite phone to contact his family and the authorities in Chile but it had not functioned well.
The ship was wrecked overnight on Thursday about 250 miles (400 kilometres) from Easter Island in a remote part of the Pacific where few boats passed.
The U.S.-flagged Stray Dog was in Easter Island when the SOS signal went out and left immediately on the rescue mission with a Chilean maritime official on board.

The Mata Rangi had a run of bad luck that began even before the journey did. Spain's Prince Felipe came for the launch in late April but it was delayed until May 5, without the prince, because of bad weather and last-minute technical hitches.
Last week, another storm nearly forced the expedition to turn back but it continued even after it lost a copper bar used for its antennae.
The expedition was backed by UNESCO as a mission to promote peace and tolerance. The Spanish royal family also supported it.
Although the raft was completely destroyed, Munoz said he is certain his brother would stage another expedition.
"I am sure he will try again," he said.
